content: 1. Co-administration of certain drugs may interfere with the therapeutic effects of immune checkpoint inhibitors. Close monitoring is advised when these drugs are used together. 2. Penicillin G benzathine can reduce the levels or effects of dienogest/estradiol valerate by altering intestinal flora. This interaction applies only to oral forms of the hormone, and the risk of contraceptive failure is low. 3. Penicillin G procaine also decreases the levels or effects of dienogest/estradiol valerate by altering intestinal flora. This interaction applies only to oral forms of the hormone, and the risk of contraceptive failure is low. 4. During concomitant use of penicillin G benzathine or procaine with oral contraceptives, an alternate or additional form of birth control may be advisable. 5. Penicillin G benzathine decreases the effects of dostarlimab, durvalumab, nivolumab, pembrolizumab, penpulimab, retifanlimab, sintilimab, tislelizumab, and toripalimab through unspecified interaction mechanisms. Close monitoring is recommended. 6. Penicillin G procaine similarly decreases the effects of these immune checkpoint inhibitors through unspecified interaction mechanisms. Close monitoring is recommended. 7. Lenolisib, an OATP1B1 and OATP1B3 inhibitor, may increase the systemic exposure of penicillin G benzathine. Avoid or use an alternative drug. 8. Penicillin G procaine decreases the effects of oral microbiota by pharmacodynamic antagonism. Avoid or use an alternative drug. Antibiotics may reduce the efficacy of oral microbiota products containing bacterial spores. Complete antibiotic regimens 2–4 days before initiating oral microbiota therapy. 9. Omadacycline and sarecycline, both tetracyclines, decrease the effects of penicillin G benzathine and procaine by pharmacodynamic antagonism. Avoid or use an alternative drug. Tetracyclines may interfere with the bactericidal action of penicillins. Monitor for reduced therapeutic effects of penicillins when used concomitantly with tetracyclines. 10. Trofinetide, an OATP1B1 and OATP1B3 inhibitor, may increase plasma levels of penicillin G benzathine. Avoid co-administration with sensitive substrates. 11. Penicillin G procaine and benzathine may increase the levels or effects of vadadustat by mechanisms involving OAT1/OAT3 inhibition. Monitor closely for excessive or rapid increases in hemoglobin response and adverse reactions. 12. Penicillin G benzathine and procaine are not indicated for the treatment of venereal diseases such as syphilis, gonorrhea, yaws, bejel, or pinta. 13. Severe pneumococcal infections, such as pneumonia, empyema, bacteremia, pericarditis, meningitis, peritonitis, and arthritis, are better treated with penicillin G sodium or potassium during the acute stage. 14. When high, sustained serum levels are required, penicillin G sodium or potassium should be administered intramuscularly (IM) or intravenously (IV). 15. The combination of penicillin G benzathine and penicillin G procaine should only be prescribed for approved indications. 16. Prescribing antibiotics in the absence of a proven or strongly suspected bacterial infection or prophylactic indication is unlikely to benefit the patient and increases the risk of developing drug-resistant bacteria. 17. Penicillin G benzathine is for deep intramuscular injection only. Inadvertent intravenous administration has been associated with cardiorespiratory arrest and death. Do not inject intravenously or mix with other intravenous solutions. 18. Administer intramuscularly in the upper outer quadrant of the buttock (dorsogluteal) or ventrogluteal site. Repeated injections into the anterolateral thigh are not recommended due to reports of quadriceps femoris fibrosis and atrophy. 19. During prolonged therapy with penicillin, particularly at high doses, periodic evaluation of renal and hematopoietic systems is recommended. 20. Antibiotic use may result in the overgrowth of non-susceptible organisms. Constant observation of the patient is essential. If new infections due to bacteria or fungi appear during therapy, discontinue the drug and take appropriate measures. 21. Reproduction studies in mice, rats, and rabbits have shown no evidence of impaired fertility or harm to the fetus due to penicillin G. Human experience with penicillins during pregnancy has not shown evidence of adverse effects on the fetus. However, there are no adequate and well-controlled studies in pregnant women to conclusively exclude harmful effects. Use during pregnancy only if clearly needed. 22. Soluble penicillin G is excreted in breast milk. Exercise caution when administering penicillin G benzathine and procaine to nursing women. 23. Penicillin G interferes with cell wall mucopeptide synthesis during active multiplication, resulting in bactericidal activity against susceptible microorganisms. 24. Do not inject penicillin G near an artery or nerve, as this may result in permanent neurologic damage. 25. For neonates, infants, and small children, the midlateral aspect of the thigh is the preferred injection site. For older children and adults, deep IM injection in the upper outer quadrant of the buttock is recommended. 26. Due to the high concentration of suspended matter, the needle may become blocked if the injection is not made at a slow, steady rate. 27. Store penicillin G refrigerated at 2–8 degrees Celsius (36–46 degrees Fahrenheit). Do not freeze. 28. Adding plans allows comparison of formulary status with other drugs in the same class. Formulary information may vary and change over time. Contact the applicable plan provider for the most current information. 29.
